newsitem.title: CHINA: Hong Kong acts to deport smuggled children.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong acts to deport smuggled children.

text.p: The Hong Kong government acted on Tuesday to deport children from China who are claiming right of abode in the territory by introducing a bill that would retroactively establish regulations for their entry.
Hong Kong has been inundated over the past year by young illegal migrants from the Chinese mainland, many now claiming right of abode here following the territory's return to China last week.

Secretary of Security Peter Lai asked the provisional legislature to rush through all three readings of a bill setting up a "certificate of eligibility" system at its first formal meeting on Wednesday to prevent a further influx.
"Any delay would be exploited by snake heads (smugglers) who would spread rumours of an amnesty and there would be the possibility of hordes of children being smuggled in," Lai said.
"At the council meeting tomorrow, I would appeal for members to have the three readings of the (bill) to tackle the emergency situation," he said.

Under the proposals, children would have to prove their eligibility to live in Hong Kong while still in China, and to receive a "certificate of eligibility" before being allowed to enter the territory.

"The amendments are going to have retrospective effect so that the Director of Immigration would be able to deal with the children who came to Hong Kong before the enactment of the ordinance (and) repatriate them back to China upon arrest," Lai said.
The smuggled children typically have at least one parent legally resident in Hong Kong and themselves have a theoretical right of abode under Hong Kong's post-handover constitution.

But a long wait, because of a huge backlog of an estimated 60,000 cases in China awaiting clearance to move to Hong Kong, has driven many families to smuggle in the children, violating frontier regulations.
Last week hundreds of families, who had been hiding smuggled children, turned in their infants to immigration authorities, believing the new government would not deport them.
The bill was approved by new Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa at his first post-handover cabinet meeting on Tuesday. Hong Kong reverted to China last week after 156 years of British rule.
While most people in Hong Kong are concerned about the influx of smuggled children, many question the wisdom and legality of retroactive legislation.
